topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Processes can exchange bytes through pipes or coordinate through shared mappings, but neither mechanism removes the need for ownership and synchronization. This Linux fixture combines a small pipe message with a process-shared semaphore protecting a shared value. The child uses a tightly bounded path and exits with _exit; the parent closes unused endpoints and reaps the child before destroying shared synchronization state.

blocks.text: A producer exits, but its consumer never sees end-of-file. The parent still owns a copied write descriptor, so the pipe remains logically open for writing. Every process performed its local work correctly; the system failed because nobody drew the complete ownership graph. Interprocess communication is as much about which references remain alive as it is about moving bytes.

blocks.text: This chapter develops two communication models. A pipe transfers a sequence of bytes through a kernel-managed channel. Shared memory lets processes access the same underlying storage, but requires a separately supported synchronization mechanism. The worked example uses both deliberately: a pipe carries a small completion message, while a process-shared semaphore coordinates access to a value in shared storage.

topics.title: 13.1.1 Creating Anonymous Pipes
topics.summary: An anonymous pipe provides a read endpoint and a write endpoint. After process creation, each process may inherit both descriptors unless they are closed or configured otherwise. Every unnecessary writer must be closed for readers to observe end-of-file when real writers finish. A forgotten inherited write descriptor can keep a reader blocked even after the intended producer exits.

blocks.text: An anonymous pipe has a read endpoint and a write endpoint represented by descriptors. It is commonly created before a child process is launched so the endpoints can be inherited or assigned through launch file actions. Each process should then retain only the endpoints required by its role. Closing unused copies is part of the protocol, not merely cosmetic cleanup. (PIPE)

blocks.text: Pipe EOF depends on the absence of remaining writer references and the consumption of buffered data. One forgotten writer in a parent, child, or executed helper can prevent EOF indefinitely. The reader cannot infer that the intended producer has finished merely because no new bytes arrived recently. Draw every inherited copy and show the point where it is closed.

blocks.text: A pipe is a byte stream, not an arbitrary message transport. Small writes within the platform’s documented atomic-write bound can have useful interleaving properties among multiple writers, but that does not mean a read returns exactly one application record. Reads can split or combine submitted byte sequences. If records matter, define framing and accumulation independently of convenient behavior observed with tiny fixtures.

blocks.text: The pipe buffer has finite capacity. A blocking writer can wait when the consumer does not drain it, and a blocking reader can wait when no data is available while a writer still exists. This creates a familiar deadlock when a parent waits for a child to exit before reading all the child’s output, while the child waits for buffer space before it can exit. Drain and supervise according to the actual dependency graph.

Socket-specific flags used later are not automatically applicable to pipe writes; the interfaces have different control options.

topics.title: 13.1.2 Building Producer-Consumer Process Pipelines
topics.summary: A producer writes data that a consumer reads, and the pipe’s bounded kernel buffer naturally creates backpressure when the consumer falls behind. A process pipeline must decide how failures propagate: an early consumer exit can cause a writer error or signal, while a producer failure can produce EOF before a complete record.

blocks.text: Close unused endpoints immediately and define a termination protocol. Do not assume that waiting for a child while leaving its output unread is safe for arbitrarily large output; the child can block on a full pipe while the parent waits for it to exit. Bound output or supervise reading and process completion together.

blocks.text: A producer-consumer process pipeline separates stages that can fail independently. The producer may parse input, the consumer may transform it, and a final stage may write output. Each link needs a byte or record contract, a capacity behavior, and a termination convention. Without those definitions, a pipeline can look correct while silently dropping a final partial record or waiting for data that will never arrive.
rich: A producer-consumer process pipeline separates stages that can fail independently. The producer may parse input, the consumer may transform it, and a final stage may write output. Each link needs a byte or record contract, a capacity behavior, and a termination convention. Without those definitions, a pipeline can look correct while silently dropping a final partial record or waiting for data that will never arrive.

blocks.text: The simplest protocol is often a bounded fixed-size control message whose complete length is known. The teaching example sends four bytes spelling done. The receiver uses exact-read logic, so a two-byte prefix followed by EOF is not accepted as completion. A real stream of variable messages needs lengths, delimiters with escaping, or another explicit framing design. Choose the protocol before selecting helper function names.

blocks.text: Backpressure occurs when a downstream stage cannot accept more data. A pipe’s finite buffer can naturally slow an upstream producer, but the surrounding application must still decide what happens if the downstream stage stops permanently. Waiting without a deadline can be appropriate for an interactive shell pipeline and inappropriate for a request with a service deadline. The context, not the pipe itself, determines the acceptable policy.

blocks.text: Failure reporting should preserve the distinction between transport completion and task success. EOF can mean the producer completed, crashed, or closed its output after an error. A separate exit status or structured terminal record may be needed. Similarly, receiving done proves that those bytes arrived; it does not automatically prove every unrelated shared-memory field has been synchronized correctly.

An operational pipeline requires ownership and cleanup for those dependencies in addition to ordinary waits and pipe closes.

topics.title: 13.2.1 Using Shared Memory
topics.summary: A shared mapping makes a region accessible to multiple processes under the operating system’s mapping semantics. Ordinary process heap pointers are not a portable shared-memory data format, because mappings can appear at different addresses in independently started processes. Use offsets or explicitly designed shared structures when addresses are not inherited at the same location.

Decide which process initializes it, when other participants may attach, how they detect partial initialization, and which participant destroys synchronization objects. blocks.text: Ordinary C++ containers generally contain process-local allocation state and pointers. Placing a std::vector object in shared memory does not automatically put its elements there or make its allocator usable from another process. A robust shared-memory container requires a specialized representation and allocation scheme whose cross-process contract is explicit. For small systems, a bounded byte-oriented record can be much easier to audit.

blocks.text: Crash recovery adds another layer. A process can die halfway through a multi-field update or while holding a process-shared lock. A protocol must decide whether partially updated state is detectable, repairable, or discarded. Shared memory improves the path by which bytes are accessed; it does not supply transactionality, durable storage, or automatic owner-death recovery.
